temperature_erratum_binding.assessment: The conversion is valid as an explicitly approximate relation between numerical values in the respective units. Removing the Celsius suffix is justified by the new definitions, not a conversion of a Kelvin quantity into a Celsius quantity. The independent alpha-convention finding below does not invalidate this local erratum.

independent_science_checks.area: Ideal versus real gas cooling and extrapolation
independent_science_checks.reasoning: For a fixed amount of ideal gas at fixed positive pressure, V=nR*Theta/p is linear in absolute temperature Theta. Its extension to zero is a model limit. A real sample's dilute-gas approximation in an appropriate range does not guarantee that cooling preserves the gas phase or the ideal relationship.
independent_science_checks.assessment: Fixed amount and constant pressure are explicit. The draft separates dilute-gas measurements and ideal extrapolation from actually shrinking the same real sample to zero volume, and preserves the original question about the meaning of that zero.

independent_science_checks.reasoning: For nonzero reference volume V0, 0=V0*(1+t/273) gives the approximate Celsius numerical value t=-273. The exact footnote gives -273.15 degrees Celsius at zero Kelvin, so exact numerical conversion is T=t+273.15; the displayed T=t+273 is the expressly marked integer approximation.
independent_science_checks.assessment: Approximate and exact values are not presented as identical exact constants. The Kelvin symbol K has no degree sign and a one-K temperature interval has the same size as a one-degree-Celsius interval.

independent_science_checks.area: Absolute zero and classical molecular-motion scope
independent_science_checks.reasoning: In the classical ideal-gas translational model, average thermal kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature, for example E=3*k_B*Theta/2, and tends to zero as Theta tends to zero. That model limit is not a statement that every form of microscopic motion in all matter stops.
independent_science_checks.assessment: The lower-limit claim is scoped to ordinary thermal-equilibrium temperature and the motion claim is explicitly classical. Lomonosov's attribution is retained as a quotation from the source, not promoted into an independently checked history claim.

independent_science_checks.reasoning: With numerical coefficient a=1/273 and numerical temperatures T=t+273, 1+a*t=1+(T-273)/273=T/273=a*T, so V=V0*a*T has the units of V0. With a physical inverse-temperature coefficient beta, beta times physical Kelvin temperature is dimensionless instead. Those are different notational conventions.
independent_science_checks.assessment: No arithmetic or fixed-amount/constant-pressure error was found. The text does not explicitly extend its numerical-value convention to alpha, which was previously given inverse-degree units; see F1.

independent_science_checks.area: Volume ratios and positive absolute temperatures
independent_science_checks.reasoning: For the same n and p, the common factor nR/p cancels, giving V1/V2=Theta1/Theta2. Using numerical values in the same Kelvin unit gives T1/T2. Celsius values do not preserve this ratio because of the additive offset.
independent_science_checks.assessment: The same amount of ideal gas, unchanged pressure, Kelvin temperatures and positive denominator are stated. No finite real-gas state at absolute zero is asserted. The ratio result is correct independently of F1's alpha notation.

findings.title: Define alpha's numerical value before combining it with numerical temperatures

source_locations.description: Alpha is given as 1/273 inverse degrees.
Modern source-bound correction expressly makes T and t numerical values.
The retained derivation includes alpha*t and alpha*T.

findings.observation: The earlier text assigns inverse-degree units to alpha. The conversion block then explicitly defines T and t as numerical values, but the derivation still multiplies them by the same alpha and merely refers back to the previously agreed values and coefficient. It never states that alpha in these numerical equations denotes the coefficient's numerical value rather than the physical inverse-temperature quantity.
findings.reasoning: Read with the declared units, alpha*t has inverse-temperature units and cannot be added to the dimensionless 1; V0*alpha*T would also not have volume units when T is a bare numerical value. The intended algebra is correct if alpha here is explicitly its numerical value 1/273. The current final sentence does not identify that change of convention.
findings.impact: A lesson explicitly teaching quantity-versus-numerical-value conversion leaves a conflicting coefficient convention in its concluding derivation. A reader following the definitions literally obtains inconsistent dimensions even though the intended numerical result is right.
findings.suggested_scoped_resolution: Add a prose-only clarification that alpha in the subsequent numerical-value equations means the numerical value 1/273 of the expansion coefficient expressed per Kelvin or per degree-Celsius interval; the physical coefficient has inverse-temperature units. Keep the source formulas, the 273 approximation, the exact footnote and the registered conversion erratum unchanged.
